item.title: Efficient LLM Pretraining: Packed Sequences and Masked Attention
item.dc:creator: Lukas Hauzenberger
item.content:encoded:
Training large language models (LLMs) is a computationally demanding task. It requires vast amounts of data, powerful hardware, and clever optimization techniques. One such technique which is not often talked about, is the use of packed sequences to fully take advantage of the chose context length in each training step.

Imagine feeding a Transformer model a batch of text sequences of varying lengths. To maintain consistent input dimensions, shorter sequences are padded with special tokens. While this seems innocuous, it wastes precious GPU memory by attending to meaningless padding tokens.

The solution: sequence packing

Packed sequences offer an elegant solution. Instead of padding, we concatenate multiple shorter sequences into a single, longer sequence. This minimizes wasted compute (through padding tokens). It also allows us to process more tokens per batch thus reducing training time. However, there’s a catch: we need to ensure the model doesn’t attend across sequence boundaries. Lets have a look at a simple example. We are packing together the following three sentences into a single sequence separated by EOS tokens.

# Setup
import torch; torch.set_printoptions(linewidth=200)
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoConfig, AutoModelForCausalLM

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("gpt2")
config = AutoConfig.from_pretrained("gpt2")
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_config(config)
sentence1 = "The cat sat on the mat"
sentence2 = "The dog ate my homework"
sentence3 = "My aunt is a teacher"

sentences = [sentence1, sentence2, sentence3]
tokenized_sentences = tokenizer(sentences, return_attention_mask=False, add_special_tokens=False)["input_ids"]
tokenized_sentences = [t for s in tokenized_sentences for t in s + [tokenizer.eos_token_id]]
tokenizer.decode(tokenized_sentences)

If we would decode the packed sequence again it would look like this:

The cat sat on the mat<|endoftext|>The dog ate my homework<|endoftext|>My aunt is a teacher<|endoftext|>

The standard attention mask for causal language modeling for the packed sequences would look like this.

tokenized_sentences = torch.tensor(tokenized_sentences)
attn_mask = torch.ones(tokenized_sentences.size(0), tokenized_sentences.size(0), dtype=torch.int).tril()
attn_mask

With this mask however, when processing the second sentence, the model can still attend to tokens in the first sentence which is not ideal as the two examples are independent. To fix this we can truncate the attention mask in a certain way. When having only one sample in the batch it is relatively easy to do in pytorch.

def get_attention_mask_for_packed_sequence(x, token_id, eos: bool = True):
    # store sequence length in variable for easier readability
    T = tokenized_sentences.size(0)
    # get indices of all EOS tokens
    eos_indices = (tokenized_sentences == tokenizer.eos_token_id).nonzero().squeeze()
    # from indices, get length of each sequence
    reps = torch.cat([eos_indices[[0]]+1, eos_indices[1:] - eos_indices[:-1]])
    # repeat each eos index n times along dimension 1 (n is the number of tokens in the sequence)
    repeated_idx = torch.repeat_interleave(eos_indices, reps).view(1,-1).expand(T, -1)
    # create tensor with all indices from 0 to T-1 repeated T times along dimesion 1
    mask_indices = torch.arange(T).view(-1,1).expand(-1, T)
    # create causal mask and additionally mask out all tokens from preceeding sequences
    mask = torch.ones(T, T, dtype=torch.bool).tril().expand(-1, -1)
    mask.masked_fill_(mask_indices > repeated_idx, False)
    return mask

get_attention_mask_for_packed_sequence(tokenized_sentences, tokenizer.eos_token_id)

As you can see, the standard causal mask is truncated to mask out tokens from previous sentences.

Adjust position ids accordingly

When packing sequences together it is important to adjust the position ids use to create position embeddings accordingly. Each token in a sequence typically has an associated position id that helps the model understand the token’s relative position. When we pack multiple sequences together, we need to ensure that the position IDs for each sequence start from the beginning (usually 0 or 1) rather than continuing from where the previous sequence left off.

By adjusting position ids we also clearly mark sequence boundaries. This is crucial for the model to distinguish between different sequences and not treat the packed data as one continuous sequence.

We can leverage the code from above function to generate the tensor with position ids

pos_ids = torch.arange(T) - torch.repeat_interleave(torch.cat([torch.tensor([0]), eos_indices+1], dim=0)[:-1], reps)
pos_ids

Attention mask for batched sequence packing

Typically during training we would like to process and entire batch of sequences. For the example code above we would have to resort to a loop implementation to get the truncated attention mask for the batch. To do it without a loop is a little bit more challenging due to the additional batch dimension. To show you how to do it lets first create a second item of packed sqeuences to get a batch of size 2.

sentence4 = "Rome wasn't built in a day"
sentence5 = "My hovercraft is full of eels"

sentences = [sentence4, sentence5]
tokenized_sentences2 = tokenizer(sentences, return_attention_mask=False, add_special_tokens=False)["input_ids"]
tokenized_sentences2 = torch.tensor([t for s in tokenized_sentences2 for t in s + [tokenizer.eos_token_id]])

batch = torch.nn.utils.rnn.pad_sequence(
  [tokenized_sentences, tokenized_sentences2],
  batch_first=True, padding_value=tokenizer.eos_token_id
)

We assign the shape of the batch to two variables B and T. This makes the following code more readable.

B, T = batch.shape

The main challenge for the batched implementation is to construct the same “repated_index” tensor like in the example from above. First we need the global indices of the EOS tokens.

eos_idx = (batch.view(-1) == tokenizer.eos_token_id) \
  .nonzero(as_tuple=True)[0] + 1

To this index vector we add the 0 index and the last token index for each batch item. This is needed to be able to separate the batch items again later on. We then remove duplicates (in case the first or last index for a batch item is already present) and sort.

eos_idx_expanded = torch.cat(
  [eos_idx, torch.arange(0,B*T+1,T)]
).unique().sort()[0]

Next since our index vector contains the global indices of EOS tokens within the batch (e.g. the forst index of the second batch item = T) we need to normalize the indices by the sequence length. For the normalized indices we replace zeros with T. This is needed in the following step.

normalized_idx = eos_idx_expanded - (eos_idx_expanded // T) * T
normalized_idx = torch.where(normalized_idx == 0, T, normalized_idx)

With the normalized indices we can check how often we need to repeat each EOS token index to get the correct sequence length. To achieve this we needed to have the last index for each sequence present. If we didnt replace 0s with T in the step beforfe the number of repetitions for the last eos index in each batch would be wrong.

reps = normalized_idx[1:] - normalized_idx[:-1]
reps = torch.where(reps < 1, normalized_idx[1:], reps)

Now we can create the batched repeated index tensor

repeated_idx = torch.repeat_interleave(
  normalized_idx[1:], reps
).view(B,1,T).expand(-1,T,-1)

The rest is similar to the example with batch size = 1. We construct a tensor with indices from 0 to T-1 repeated T times along dimension 1 and create a causal mask. We then mask out all tokens from preceeding sequences.

mask_indices = torch.arange(T).view(1,-1,1).expand(B, -1, T)
# create mask
mask = torch.ones(T, T, dtype=torch.bool).tril().expand(B, -1, -1)
mask = mask.masked_fill(mask_indices >= repeated_idx, False)

Here is the full function. I added to possiblity to chose between checking eos tokens or bos tokens.

def get_attention_mask_for_packed_sequence(x, token_id, eos: bool = True):
    B, T = x.shape
    eos_idx = (x.view(-1) == token_id).nonzero(as_tuple=True)[0] + eos
    eos_idx_expanded = torch.cat([eos_idx, torch.arange(0,B*T+1,T)]).unique().sort()[0]
    normalized_idx = eos_idx_expanded - (eos_idx_expanded // T) * T
    normalized_idx = torch.where(normalized_idx == 0, T, normalized_idx)
    reps = normalized_idx[1:] - normalized_idx[:-1]
    reps = torch.where(reps < 1, normalized_idx[1:], reps)
    repeated_idx = torch.repeat_interleave(normalized_idx[1:], reps).view(B,1,T).expand(-1,T,-1)
    mask_indices = torch.arange(T).view(1,-1,1).expand(B, -1, T)
    mask = torch.ones(T, T, dtype=torch.bool).tril().expand(B, -1, -1)
    mask = mask.masked_fill(mask_indices >= repeated_idx, False)
    return mask

Analogously to the example above without a batch dimension you can reuse the code for creating the attention mask to get the correct position ids:

pos_ids = (torch.arange(B*T) - torch.repeat_interleave(eos_idx_expanded[:-1], reps)).view(B,T)
pos_ids

You can also find all code snippets in this notebook.

item.title: Introducing pytora — a minimal PyTorch implementation of LoRA
item.dc:creator: Lukas Hauzenberger
item.content:encoded:
Introducing pytora — a minimal PyTorch implementation of LoRA

TLDR - here is the code: https://github.com/sirluk/pytora

Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has emerged as a game-changing technique in the realm of large language model fine-tuning. By significantly reducing the number of trainable parameters, LoRA makes adapting massive models to specific tasks or domains more computationally feasible and efficient. Its elegant approach, which injects trainable rank decomposition matrices into existing model layers, has led to widespread adoption across research and industry. The success of LoRA is also evident in the number of variations it inspired: LoRA+, DoRA, VeRA, AdaLoRA, Delta-LoRA, MoRA and many more.

If you are reading this, chances are you have already used LoRA for one or the other task. Probably the most common way to integrate LoRA into ones training code is probably through the 🤗 PEFT library. However, you might prefer an alternative approach for various reasons, such as

  1. Limited Flexibility: PEFT provides a streamlined way to apply LoRA to specific model architectures and tasks. However, it may not offer the same level of customisation or control as a manual implementation, especially for researchers who want to experiment with variations of LoRA or apply it to less common architectures.
  2. Potential Performance Overhead: In some cases, the abstractions and convenience features of PEFT might introduce a slight performance overhead compared to a highly optimised, bare-bones implementation of LoRA. For applications where maximising computational efficiency is critical, this overhead could be a factor.
  3. Dependency on Hugging Face Ecosystem: PEFT is deeply integrated with the 🤗 Transformers library and ecosystem. While this is convenient for users who already work within that framework, it could be a drawback for those who prefer other libraries or want to avoid additional dependencies.

I created this guide to provide an easy alternative to PEFT.

pytora for LoRA

Since Pytorch 1.9 there is a very elegant way to implement LoRA with vanilla PyTorch code: PyTorch parametrizations. They act like forward pre-hooks and allow you to define operations for weights that are executed before each forward pass. For details I recommend the official tutorial which helped me a lot for the first implementation.

In pytora LoRA adapters are implemented this way. A LoRA layer is defined as a standard torch Module and then applied to each weight matrix which we want to finetune.

import torch
from torch import nn
from torch.nn.utils.parametrize import register_parametrization
import math


class LoraLayer(nn.Module):

    def __init__(self, weight, r, alpha = 1, dropout_prob = 0, fan_in_fan_out = False):
        super().__init__()

        if fan_in_fan_out:
            self.in_features = weight.shape[0]
            self.out_features = weight.shape[1]
        else:
            self.in_features = weight.shape[1]
            self.out_features = weight.shape[0]
        self.alpha = alpha
        self.fan_in_fan_out = fan_in_fan_out

        if dropout_prob > 0.:
            self.lora_dropout = nn.Dropout(p=dropout_prob)
        else:
            self.lora_dropout = nn.Identity()

        self._init_lora(r, weight_dtype=weight.dtype)

    def _init_lora(self, r, weight_dtype = None):
        # Actual trainable parameters
        if r > 0:
            if weight_dtype == None:
                weight_dtype = self.lora_A.dtype
            self.register_parameter(
                'lora_A',
                nn.Parameter(torch.empty((self.in_features, r), dtype=weight_dtype))
            )
            self.register_parameter(
                'lora_B',
                nn.Parameter(torch.zeros((r, self.out_features), dtype=weight_dtype))
            )
            self.scaling = self.alpha / r
            nn.init.kaiming_uniform_(self.lora_A, a=math.sqrt(5))
        else:
            try:
                # ensure parameters do not exist if they are zero
                delattr(self, "lora_A")
                delattr(self, "lora_B")
                delattr(self, "scaling")
            except AttributeError:
                pass
        self.r = r

    def change_lora_rank(self, new_rank):
        if new_rank != self.r:
            self._init_lora(new_rank)

    def forward(self, X):
        if self.r == 0:
            return X
        else:
            lora = self.lora_dropout(self.lora_A @ self.lora_B * self.scaling)
            if not self.fan_in_fan_out:
                lora = lora.T
            return X + lora


# example for applying a lora adapter

module = torch.nn.Linear(10,10)

adapter = LoraLayer(weight = module.weight, r = 4)

register_parametrization(module, "weight", adapter)

If you install pytora into your environment you can add LoRA adapters to all or only a subset of the layers in your model with only one line of code.

from transformers import AutoModel
from pytora import apply_lora

model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B")

# OPTION 1: apply to all layers
apply_lora(model, lora_r = 4)

# OPTION 2: apply to subset explicit
apply_lora(model, lora_r = 4, names_to_include = ["q_proj", "k_proj"])

# OPTION 3: apply to subset implicit
apply_lora(model, lora_r = 4, names_to_exclude = ["lm_head"])

If you just want to use vanilla PyTorch and dont want to install pytora even though it has no dependencies other than “torch>=1.9.0” you can of course also just copy/paste the LoRA module definition and call register_parametrizations in your own code.

What’s Next for pytora?

This is just the beginning for pytora. I have ambitious plans to expand its capabilities, including:

  • More flexible LoRA adapters: Support for merged QKV layers and other transformer architectures.
  • Other LoRA variants: Implementations of proven methods like LoRA+, DoRA, and others.
  • Performance optimizations: Make pytora even faster and more efficient.

If you’re excited about applying LoRA with vanilla PyTorch, I invite you to join me in improving pytora. Check out the GitHub repository, contribute your ideas and code, or simply share your feedback.

item.title: Multilabel Classification using Mistral-7B on a single GPU with quantization and LoRA
item.dc:creator: Lukas Hauzenberger
item.content:encoded:
LLMs have impressed with there abilities to solve a wide variety of tasks, not only for natural language but also in a multimodal setting. Due to their size (“smaller” LLMs still have > 1 billion parameters) and hardware requirements it is not easy to finetune them out of the box for people without a large compute budget. However, there are techniques that can reduce the number of parameters and improve the efficiency of these models, such as LoRA and quantization. In this article, I will demonstrate how to use these techniques with the Huggingface (HF) libraries transformers, bitsandbytes and peft, which provide Python implementations of these methods. I will also show you how to apply Mistal 7b, a state-of-the-art LLM, to a multiclass classification task.

This guide is by no means the first of its kind and there are other great resource that go over this topic such as this one. Nevertheless I did not find any specific resources on multiclass classification which is why I hope this article is of interest to some. The python script from which the code samples below are taken can be found here: https://github.com/sirluk/llm_finetuning/tree/main/llm_multilabel_clf

Imports

All required imports for the code snippets below

import os
import random
import functools
import csv
import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from sklearn.metrics import f1_score
from skmultilearn.model_selection import iterative_train_test_split
from datasets import Dataset, DatasetDict
from peft import (
    LoraConfig,
    prepare_model_for_kbit_training,
    get_peft_model
)
from transformers import (
    AutoModelForSequenceClassification,
    AutoTokenizer,
    BitsAndBytesConfig,
    TrainingArguments,
    Trainer
)

Dataset

We will be using this Kaggle dataset on Topic Modeling for Research Articles based on title and abstract.

Example

ID: 5
TITLE: Comparative study of Discrete Wavelet Transforms and Wavelet Tensor Train decomposition to feature extraction of FTIR data of medicinal plants
ABSTRACT: Fourier-transform infra-red (FTIR) spectra of samples from 7 plant species were used to explore the influence of preprocessing and feature extraction on efficiency of machine learning algorithms. …
Computer Science: 1
Physics: 0
Mathematics: 0
Statistics: 1
Quantitative Biology: 0
Quantitative Finance: 0

We create a HF dataset from train.csv as this is required later on when using other functions/classes from HF libraries.

# set random seed
random.seed(0)

# load data
with open('train.csv', newline='') as csvfile:
    data = list(csv.reader(csvfile, delimiter=','))
    header_row = data.pop(0)

# shuffle data
random.shuffle(data)

# reshape
idx, text, labels = list(zip(*[(int(row[0]), f'Title: {row[1].strip()}\n\nAbstract: {row[2].strip()}', row[3:]) for row in data]))
labels = np.array(labels, dtype=int)

# create label weights
label_weights = 1 - labels.sum(axis=0) / labels.sum()

# stratified train test split for multilabel ds
row_ids = np.arange(len(labels))
train_idx, y_train, val_idx, y_val = iterative_train_test_split(row_ids[:,np.newaxis], labels, test_size = 0.1)
x_train = [text[i] for i in train_idx.flatten()]
x_val = [text[i] for i in val_idx.flatten()]

# create hf dataset
ds = DatasetDict({
    'train': Dataset.from_dict({'text': x_train, 'labels': y_train}),
    'val': Dataset.from_dict({'text': x_val, 'labels': y_val})
})

One slightly exotic package used in this snippet is probably skmultilearn which I exclusively use for the function iterative_train_test_split. This creates an even split for unbalanced multilabel datasets which is the case for this example as you can see in the visualization below. Therefore we also generate weights for our labels which we later use for calculating the loss because we would like to assign higher weights to underrepresented classes. The use of a weighted loss function is of course very dependent on your use case and the cost of trading off global accuracy vs individual class accuracy.

Initialize the model

Next we initialize our model and tokenizer. As already mentioned in the introduction we will use Mistral 7b which showed great results on a wide variety of nlp benchmarks. The code below should however work for any decoder-only LLM from the HF hub.

For finetuning we use LoRA to learn two lower dimensional diff matrices instead of having to finetune the full parameter matrix. You can find more details about lora in the paper. Since we do not need to change the pre-trained parameters during finetuning with LoRA we can quantize them using the bitsandbytes library from HF. In addition to our model we of course also need to intialize a tokenizer to preprocess our dataset.

# model name
model_name = 'mistralai/Mistral-7B-v0.1'

# preprocess dataset with tokenizer
def tokenize_examples(examples, tokenizer):
    tokenized_inputs = tokenizer(examples['text'])
    tokenized_inputs['labels'] = examples['labels']
    return tokenized_inputs

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
tokenizer.pad_token = tokenizer.eos_token
tokenized_ds = ds.map(functools.partial(tokenize_examples, tokenizer=tokenizer), batched=True)
tokenized_ds = tokenized_ds.with_format('torch')

# qunatization config
quantization_config = BitsAndBytesConfig(
    load_in_4bit = True, # enable 4-bit quantization
    bnb_4bit_quant_type = 'nf4', # information theoretically optimal dtype for normally distributed weights
    bnb_4bit_use_double_quant = True, # quantize quantized weights //insert xzibit meme
    bnb_4bit_compute_dtype = torch.bfloat16 # optimized fp format for ML
)

# lora config
lora_config = LoraConfig(
    r = 16, # the dimension of the low-rank matrices
    lora_alpha = 8, # scaling factor for LoRA activations vs pre-trained weight activations
    target_modules = ['q_proj', 'k_proj', 'v_proj', 'o_proj'],
    lora_dropout = 0.05, # dropout probability of the LoRA layers
    bias = 'none', # wether to train bias weights, set to 'none' for attention layers
    task_type = 'SEQ_CLS'
)

# load model
model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(
    model_name,
    quantization_config=quantization_config,
    num_labels=labels.shape[1]
)
model = prepare_model_for_kbit_training(model)
model = get_peft_model(model, lora_config)
model.config.pad_token_id = tokenizer.pad_token_id

As you can see from target_modules in LoraConfig we only apply finetuning to the attention weights. This works quite well and is more parameter efficient as the biggest share of parameters in a Transformer layer comes from the FeedForward Network which we freeze and quantize. r is the dimensionality of the LoRA matrices which in our case are 4096x16 and 16x4096, quite a bit smaller than the full 4096x4096 weight matrices in the Mistral attention layers.

The HF class AutoModelForSequenceClassification initializes the base model with an additional (untrained) linear classification layer on top of the last token embedding. This layer is automatically excluded from quantization and we finetune it with the rest of the LoRA weights.

Training

We are almost ready to finetune our model with the HF Trainer class, after preparing our dataset and setting up our model configuration. But before we do that, we have to define some custom functions that our trainer will use.

  1. Data Collator
    We need to tell the trainer how it should preprocess batches coming from the dataset before they can be passed to the model.
  2. Metrics
    We furthermore need pass a function to the trainer which defines the evaluation metrics we want to compute in addition to the loss.
# define custom batch preprocessor
def collate_fn(batch, tokenizer):
    dict_keys = ['input_ids', 'attention_mask', 'labels']
    d = {k: [dic[k] for dic in batch] for k in dict_keys}
    d['input_ids'] = torch.nn.utils.rnn.pad_sequence(
        d['input_ids'], batch_first=True, padding_value=tokenizer.pad_token_id
    )
    d['attention_mask'] = torch.nn.utils.rnn.pad_sequence(
        d['attention_mask'], batch_first=True, padding_value=0
    )
    d['labels'] = torch.stack(d['labels'])
    return d

# define which metrics to compute for evaluation
def compute_metrics(p):
    predictions, labels = p
    f1_micro = f1_score(labels, predictions > 0, average = 'micro')
    f1_macro = f1_score(labels, predictions > 0, average = 'macro')
    f1_weighted = f1_score(labels, predictions > 0, average = 'weighted')
    return {
        'f1_micro': f1_micro,
        'f1_macro': f1_macro,
        'f1_weighted': f1_weighted
    }

Furthermore we also need to define a custom trainer class to be able to calculate our multilabel loss which treats each output neuron as a binary classification instance. To be able to use our label weights for the loss we also need to define it as a class attribute in the __init__ method so the compute_loss method has access to it.

# create custom trainer class to be able to pass label weights and calculate mutilabel loss
class CustomTrainer(Trainer):

    def __init__(self, label_weights, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.label_weights = label_weights
    
    def compute_loss(self, model, inputs, return_outputs=False):
        labels = inputs.pop("labels")
        
        # forward pass
        outputs = model(**inputs)
        logits = outputs.get("logits")
        
        # compute custom loss
        loss = F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(logits, labels.to(torch.float32), pos_weight=self.label_weights)
        return (loss, outputs) if return_outputs else loss

Now everything is ready and we can let HF do its magic. (depending on your GPU memory you might need/want to adjust the batch size, this was tested on a GPU with 16gb RAM)

# define training args
training_args = TrainingArguments(
    output_dir = 'multilabel_classification',
    learning_rate = 1e-4,
    per_device_train_batch_size = 8,
    per_device_eval_batch_size = 8,
    num_train_epochs = 10,
    weight_decay = 0.01,
    evaluation_strategy = 'epoch',
    save_strategy = 'epoch',
    load_best_model_at_end = True
)

# train
trainer = CustomTrainer(
    model = model,
    args = training_args,
    train_dataset = tokenized_ds['train'],
    eval_dataset = tokenized_ds['val'],
    tokenizer = tokenizer,
    data_collator = functools.partial(collate_fn, tokenizer=tokenizer),
    compute_metrics = compute_metrics,
    label_weights = torch.tensor(label_weights, device=model.device)
)

trainer.train()

# save model
peft_model_id = 'multilabel_mistral'
trainer.model.save_pretrained(peft_model_id)
tokenizer.save_pretrained(peft_model_id)

Thats it! You just finetuned a state-of-the-art LLM for multilabel classification. You can load your saved model with this snippet take from the HF docs.

# load model
peft_model_id = 'multilabel_mistral'
model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(peft_model_id)

I hope with this article I was able to shed some light on how to leverage HF implentations of compute and memory efficient techniques such as LoRA and quantization for a finetuning task. From my experience there is alot of documentation about this for the most straightforward use cases but as soon as you requirements deviate a bit some adaptions are required such as defining a custom Trainer class.

item.title: What I learned doing Data Science Interviews in the 2020s
item.dc:creator: Lukas Hauzenberger
item.content:encoded:
Few disciplines have experienced hype periods comparable to that of Data Science (DS) and Machine Learning (ML) since approximately 2016. The demand for new data scientists has soared paralleled by the continuous stream of new talent and people looking for a career switch entering into the field. Due to the growing importance of DS for businesses and the higher volume of applicants for DS positions, interview processes have gotten more refined and challenging.

Nevertheless, I believe that effective preparation can provide a substantial competitive advantage for many open positions, despite maybe having only a basic understanding of Statistics and ML. In this article, I will share key insights I gained from participating in a significant double-digit number of DS interviews over the past few years — both as an applicant and as part of the hiring team.

First tip: pimp your CV!

This might be obvious but having a good CV that makes you stand out vs hundreds of other applicants is essential. Without being invited for an interview you cannot apply any of the other tips I will give you. A good CV combines effective formatting/design with compelling content.

For formatting I highly recommend this LaTeX template which can be used for both a CV as well as a cover letter (if you want to bother with that). In case you dont know LaTeX I highly encourage you to learn it as its incredibly useful to write any kind of longer technical documents. For anyone with some coding knowledge, which I would assume you have, its pretty easy to pick up.

For optimizing the CV content I wont go too much in detail since there is already a lot of specialized guides available but the three tips I would give you are the following:

  • Tell a consistent story. The different roles you list in your CV should make sense in the sequence you present them. If you list a non-senior position after a senior position you will likely raise question marks. As job titles are anyway not really comparable across companies (everyone has their own naming schema) I would suggest to tweak the labels you give to the roles on your CV to tell a consistent story of career growth.
  • Emphasize proficiency in programming languages, data manipulation, and machine learning frameworks. Provide concrete examples of impactful projects to demonstrate the practical application of those skills. Also quantify achievements wherever possible, using metrics to highlight the impact of your contributions.
  • Tailor your CV to the specific job by aligning your skills and experiences with the requirements of the role. I cannot state the advantage of this enough. Recruiters often hire for a position in a specific team therefore they often know which technologies, frameworks and algorithms you will be working with and will skim CVs for keywords related to that. Its usually easy to extract information on that from the job posting.

The case study

A case study is a popular method to weed out impostors that might be able to present themselves well but do not have the skills to back it up. In my experience it often comes after a first screening call where your technical knowledge is never tested and before the second round interview where usually a SME is present who can challenge your DS knowledge.

Typically a case study involves a dataset with company pseudo data and some DS problem statement. The goal of such assignments is almost never to achieve the best model performance and somehow amaze with an extremely low error metric but to get some insight in your way of working and if you follow generally accepted best practices for the development process. In my opinion there are some key points you should consider when working on such a case study:

  • Clarify open questions early: We all like to procrastinate so it does happen quite often that an applicant starts working on on the evening of the deadline. It is fine if you do this but make sure you at least quickly read through the case study as soon as you get it to have enough time to clarify any important points with your company contact person.
  • Make your assumptions transparent: If your approach assumes anything that is not clearly stated in the case description you should list those assumptions when you present your results.
  • Exploratory data analysis is important: I have experienced multiple times that the dataset you get contains some traps such as features that are just random noise, extreme outliers or highly imbalanced data. Things like this are easily detected by just generating some basic plots about the data distribution. Doing this requires little effort but skipping this step can quickly disqualify you in the eyes of the interviewer.
  • Train / Validation / Test split: Everyone who has done some basic crash course in data science knows about doing a train-test split but many often forget that when running different models and/or trying different values for hyperparameters you run into danger of overfitting on the test data. Therefore it is important to keep a third subset of the data that you do the final evaluation on once you have selected your best model and hyperparameters. This is generally referred to as the test set while the dataset you perform your intermediate evaluations on is the validation set. If you do not follow this pattern there is a high chance it will be addressed during the interview.
  • Create a baseline model: many make the mistake of directly jumping to xgboost or a neural network for something were linear / logistic regression might have provided similar or even better performance. For timeseries problems make sure you check the performance of just predicting the last value. I once had a candiate explain to me he selected an LSTM for a time series case study because its a simple model. He was then unable to explain to me how an LSTM works. This leads me to my next point.
  • Know the algorithm you are using! Chances are you will be asked to explain how it works and why you chose it. If you are aware of this before the interview it is relatively easy to prepare good answers. Therefore be aware of the advantages and disadvantages of the algorithm and know about the most important hyperparameters.
  • Feature Importance: It is not essential but generally well received if you somehow visualise the importance of different features for you model. Some model implementation have built in methods that give out feature importances so it is very little effort to apply this. An alternative would be to use Shapely values.

Technical Interview

In addition to being questioned about the case study, for which I hope you are well-prepared using the tips provided in the preceding section, I’d like to highlight some popular topics that often serve as sources for data science interview questions.

  • Bias Variance Tradeoff: Know about the dangers of overfitting and that it visually equates to the training error decreasing while the validation error increases. Also have in mind that overfitting equates to high variance while underfitting equates to high bias which is usually the case with simple models (e.g. the mean which is essentially a very simple statistical model). Ideally also know how the mean squared error can be represented with bias and variance.
  • Linear Regression and OLS: Linear regression is one of the simplest models and it is a popular topic for interviews to see if you know the basics. Therfore you should be able to explain the model in detail. You should also know OLS, in particular its assumptions.
  • Maximum Likelihood Estimation: It involves maximizing the likelihood function for a specific statistical model (e.g. Gaussian Distribution). The goal is to optimize the parameters of the statistical model so that they make the observed data most probable. The likelihood function quantifies the probability of observing the given data given the parameter values. Also be aware that for linear models maximum likelihood estimation is equivalent to OLS.
  • Bayes Theorem: Be able to explain what bayes theorem says and what its components are. For more challenging interviews be prepared to solve a simple mathematical example such as this one using bayes theorem.
  • Confusion Matrix and F1 Score: A confusion matrix helps visulalise the performance of a classification algorithm. You should know what precision and recall are and why the F1 score is suitable for imablanced classification but accuracy is not.
  • Imbalanced classification: How to deal with imbalanced classes (sampling techniques such as boostrapping, random duplication, SMOTE, stratified train-test split or weighted loss functions). Have an idea about which algorithms perform well out of the box on imbalanced data (GBM) and suitable evaluation metrics (F1 score).
  • Unsupervised learning: Know about examples of unsupervised learning (Clustering, Anomaly Detection, Dimensionality Reduction). Know about popular algorithms (K-Means, DB-SCAN, Expectation Maximisation for clustering; Isolation Forest, One-Class SVM for anomaly detection; t-SNE, UMAP for dimensionality reduction). For clustering you should also know about the elbow method.
  • Imputation: Be able to explain what imputation is and in what cases it makes sense. Name at least one imputation technique: Mean imputation, Hot/Cold deck imputation, Regression Imputation
  • Data Drift: Know what data drift is and how you can measure it (KL divergence, Wasserstein distance)
  • Neural Networks: Be able to explain how a neural network works and know about widely used neural network components (though I feel like this is not asked too frequently in detail)
    Optimizers: SGD, SGD with Momentum, Adam
    Regularization Techniques: L1, L2, Dropout
    Activation Functions: Tanh, ReLU
    Special Layers: Embeddings, attention, residual / skip connections
    The Vanishing Gradient Problem and how to fix it (e.g. with Residual Layers, Batch/Layer Norm, ReLU)
  • Know your interviewer: Before an interview you will usually get a calendar invite or an email where the names of the people that will participate in the meeting are already listed. You can use this to check online (LinkedIn, personal website etc.) what projects/topics they have already worked on in the past and what their interests are. This can be invaluable information when preparing for an interview because based on the job description and the interviews interests you can often get a good idea what likely questions could be and which topics you should refresh your knowledge on.
    Also be aware that if the interviewers interests align with something that you mentioned in your CV or cover letter it is very likely they will ask you about it.

Final thoughts

In this article I tried to give an overview of the most important components of a DS interview. From my experience if you know the topics that are listed here well and follow my suggestions you should be very well prepared for 95 percent of DS interview processes. Of course for very specialised roles or research related positions the process and questions might look very different. I would be very interested to hear your thoughts on this and if there is topics / tips I missed which from your experience should be included in this guide.

If you would like a additional guidance for mastering DS interviews or have more specific questions you are also welcome to send me a message at lukas.hauzenberger.medium@gmail.com

item.title: Training and serving PyTorch models in the Google Cloud with Vertex AI pipelines
item.dc:creator: Lukas Hauzenberger
item.content:encoded:
With each new feature Vertex AI is making it easier to put Machine Learning (ML) prototypes into production. Nowadays you do not really need to be a ML Ops expert anymore to develop production grade pipelines in the Google Cloud Platform (GCP).

However, while there are many tools in the GCP that make it easier for Data Scientists and ML Experts to do ML Ops, the variety of tools can be a bit overwhelming. Furthermore PyTorch is becoming more and more popular with each iteration and many google services still primarily support Tensorflow or at least make it much easier to implement something when the code is written in Tensorflow. Therefore I feel like a guide like this could help many PyTorch fans. It will give you step-by-step instructions on how to automatically train and deploy a PyTorch model in the GCP with Vertex AI pipelines. All code can be found here.

There is an older google blog post which helped me setting up the first pipeline but it doesn’t go too much in depth about many of the steps required for setting up such a pipeline. Nevertheless I want to share this article here as well: google blog post

Which GCP services do we need?

Before we start with the step-by-step guide, I will briefly go over all the GCP services I will use and what I will use them for. If you want to do a 1:1 implementation make sure you have access to these first. If you are familiar with the GCP you can probably skip this chapter. To get a first impression how these services are integrated in a pipeline I made a high level visualization.

Cloud Scheduler

A cron job scheduler which we will use to define a model training schedule. It can invoke any service with a http trigger functionality. We will use it to trigger a cloud function which will compile and run the Vertex AI pipeline.

Cloud Functions

The go-to service to run lightweight applications in the GCP. The main advantage compared to Cloud Run is that it does not require any boilerplate code to define container environments. We will use it as a pipeline initiator by setting up a Python function that triggers a Vertex AI pipeline with given hyperparameters.

Vertex AI

Vertex AI is an umbrella term for several GCP tools related to ML Ops. We will use five different Vertex AI tools:

  • Pipelines
    Vertex AI Pipelines is a tool to orchestrate ML workflows. It consists of one or more pipeline components, where each component is a self-contained set of code that performs one part of a pipeline’s workflow. The flow of the pipeline (i.e. which components are executed in what order) can be configured in Python using the Kubeflow SDK. You can use pre-built components or define your own and there are different ways to define custom components. For example you can create custom Python packages or just create a Python function for each component. You can read more about how to build components here.
  • Training
    We won’t use a pipeline component for training our model but a Vertex AI training job. In a later chapter I will explain the reason why.
  • Tensorboard instance
    Vertex AI TensorBoard instances can be used to log experiments. They are quite expensive (300 $ / month for one instance) and using them is completely optional as it is also possible to log experiments in some other custom way.
  • Model registry
    Is a central location to manage and organize all you models and versions. If we want to expose a model as an endpoint or use it for batch prediction runs we need to first store it in the model registry.
  • Endpoints
    We have two options to use our trained ML model for inference. Via batch prediction jobs or as a model endpoint which can do online-processing of single inference requests. For this tutorial we will expose the trained model as an endpoint. (HINT: When using Vertex AI endpoints it is important to consider the costs as the endpoint will be continuously online, and depending on the machine type this can get expensive.)

Cloud Build

Cloud build is a serverless CI/CD platform. We will use it to build the docker containers for our pipeline components.

Artifact Registry

Artifact registry is a place to manage container images which is exactly what we will use it for.

Cloud Storage

Cloud storage is the blob storage service in the GCP. It is also integrated with most other GCP tools to store artifacts and results and probably the GCP tool I use the most. For our pipeline we will use Cloud Storage for multiple purposes: storing training data, working directory for Vertex AI pipelines and storing outputs such as the trained model.

Building the pipeline

As the first part of our step-by-step guide, lets go over how we define our Vertex AI pipeline. For the definition we create a file “pipeline.py” containing component and flow definition. In our case we define each of the components as a function, the code for which is stored in separate subfolders within the directory containing “pipeline.py”. Additionally we need the Kubeflow SDK to define the pipeline steps. Our import section for “pipeline.py” looks like this:

from kfp import dsl
from kfp import components as comp

from .components.train_model.main import train_model
from .components.build_model.main import build_model
from .components.deploy_model.main import deploy_model
from .components.save_model_info.main import save_model_info

We then use the “create_component_from_func” function from the Kubeflow SDK to package each Python function as a component. For that we need to specify a Python version for the component as well as all required packages. Here is an example how this looks for the “train_model” component:

train_model_op_fun = (
    comp.create_component_from_func(
        train_model,
        packages_to_install=[
            "kfp==1.8.18",
            "fire==0.4.0",
            "gcsfs==2022.11.0",
            "google-cloud-aiplatform==1.20.0"
        ],
        base_image="python:3.9.16"
    )
)

Once we defined our components like this we need to specify the order in which these components should be executed in the pipeline. To do this we setup a main pipeline function with the Kubeflow decorator “@dsl.pipeline”. Here we can also define where additional input parameters to component functions are coming from. Using Kubeflow commands we furthermore define container hardware requirements for each container. It is important to note here is that we cannot use variables within the pipeline definition so the machine configuration needs to be hardcoded in the script. This can be an issue when we want to have a flexible pipeline which depending on the model architecture can run with different machine configurations. There is a workaround to this with Vertex AI which we will discuss in the next chapter where we look into each component in more detail.

train_model

def train_model(
    comp_params: dict
) -> NamedTuple('train_model_outputs', [
    ('DUMMY', str)
]):
    
    import argparse
    from google.cloud import aiplatform
    
    cfg = argparse.Namespace(**comp_params)
        
    # trainer image
    trainer_image_uri = f'{cfg.build_location}-docker.pkg.dev/{cfg.project_id}/{cfg.trainer_image_name}/{cfg.trainer_image_name}'
    
    trainer_args = [
        f'--base-dir={cfg.working_dir}',
        f'--model-dir={cfg.working_dir}/{cfg.model_dir}',
        f'--training-data-uri={cfg.bucket}/train_data/{cfg.language}/ds_train.csv',
        f'--validation-data-uri={cfg.bucket}/train_data/{cfg.language}/ds_validation.csv',
        '--data-format=gcs',
        f'--language={cfg.language}',
        f'--model_name={cfg.model_name}',
        f'--model_name_output={cfg.model_name_output}',
        f'--lr={cfg.lr}',
        f'--dropout={cfg.dropout}',
        f'--n_hidden={cfg.n_hidden}',
        f'--batch_size={cfg.batch_size}',
        f'--num_epochs={cfg.num_epochs}',
        f'--val_size={cfg.val_size}',
        f'--output_file_label_map={cfg.output_file_label_map}'
    ]
    
    try:
        debug = eval(cfg.debug.lower())
    except (NameError, AttributeError) as e:
        print(repr(e))
        debug = False   
    if debug: trainer_args.append('--debug')
    
    tensorboard_resource_name = f'projects/{cfg.project_id}/locations/{cfg.model_location}/tensorboards/{cfg.tensorboard_id}'

    aiplatform.init(project=cfg.project_id, location=cfg.model_location, staging_bucket=cfg.bucket)
    
    display_name_parts = [
        cfg.dt,
        cfg.language,
        cfg.model_name,
        cfg.batch_size,
        cfg.lr
    ]
    job = aiplatform.CustomContainerTrainingJob(
        display_name = "_".join([str(x) for x in display_name_parts]),
        container_uri = trainer_image_uri + ':latest'
    )

    model = job.run(
        args = trainer_args,
        base_output_dir = cfg.working_dir,
        replica_count = int(cfg.trainer_replica_count),
        machine_type = cfg.trainer_machine_type,
        accelerator_type = cfg.trainer_gpu_type,
        accelerator_count = int(cfg.trainer_n_gpu),
        tensorboard = tensorboard_resource_name,
        service_account = cfg.service_account,
        sync = True
    )
    
    return ("DONE",)

As the name suggests the train_model component performs model training based on the provided training data. One challenge we have here is that we would like to be able to train an arbitrary model and different model architectures have different hardware requirements for training. As we found out in the previous chapter container machine configurations need to be hardcoded in the “pipeline.py” script and it is not possible to pass values through variables. A workaround for this is that we define a “meta” container which executes a Vertex AI training job using the aiplatform.CustomContainerTrainingJob class. This class allows us to define variable hardware requirements for the training job and itself creates and runs another container. The architecture looks something like this:

The two main components of the train_model container are:

  • Defining a list of arguments to pass to the Vertex AI training pipeline
  • Initiating and running a Vertex AI custom container training job

Within the train_model component folder you will find a subfolder “trainer_image”. This directory contains all information needed to build the container for the Vertex AI training job. There are already quite a few tutorials out there on how to do custom training in Vertex AI so I won’t go too much in detail about the structure here (for example).

In our example the code instantiates and trains a PyTorch model. We also do not have all our code stored in a single file but, as is usually the case with production grade ML pipelines, have a subdirectory “helpers” with additional .py files. This will become important in the next chapter when we create our container for model serving.

Once finished, the Vertex AI training job saves all model files into a specified Google Cloud Storage bucket.

build_model

def build_model(
    comp_params: dict,
) -> NamedTuple('build_model_outputs', [
    ('endpoint_image_uri', str),
    ('commit_sha', str)
]):

    import os
    import argparse
    from google.cloud.devtools import cloudbuild
    
    cfg = argparse.Namespace(**comp_params)
    
    endpoint_image_uri = f"{cfg.build_location}-docker.pkg.dev/{cfg.project_id}/{cfg.endpoint_image_name}/{cfg.endpoint_image_name}_{cfg.language}"

    client = cloudbuild.CloudBuildClient()
    
    request = cloudbuild.RunBuildTriggerRequest(
        project_id = cfg.project_id,
        trigger_id = cfg.trigger_name,
        # https://cloud.google.com/python/docs/reference/cloudbuild/latest/google.cloud.devtools.cloudbuild_v1.types.RepoSource
        source = {
            "branch_name": cfg.repo_branch,
            "dir_": cfg.build_dir,
            "substitutions": {
                "_IMG_URI": endpoint_image_uri,
                "_MODEL_DIR": f"{cfg.working_dir}/{cfg.model_dir}",
                "_TRAINER_CODE_DIR": cfg.trainer_code_dir,
                "_BUILD_DIR": cfg.build_dir,
                "_MODEL_NAME": cfg.endpoint_model_name,
                "_LABEL_MAP_FILE": cfg.output_file_label_map
            }
        }
    )

    operation = client.run_build_trigger(request=request)
    
    response = operation.result()
    
    return (endpoint_image_uri, response.substitutions["COMMIT_SHA"])

Once our model is trained, what we want to do is package it into a container so that it can be used by Vertex AI for inference. There is a list of prebuilt container images that can be used for model serving in Vertex AI.

Dockerfile

Unfortunately at least at the time of writing the pre-built container images for PyTorch did not contain the transformers library thus making them unusable for many NLP tasks. We therefore need to define a custom container image for PyTorch model serving. In the following I will explain in detail how to set up a Dockerfile for such a container.

PyTorch models are served via TorchServe, therefore we pull the latest base image. Since we might want to use a gpu also for inference we pull an image with gpu support.

FROM pytorch/torchserve:latest-gpu

We will user the root user to upgrade pip and setuptools to the latest version (some commands can only be executed by the root user).

USER root
RUN pip3 install --upgrade pip
RUN pip3 install --upgrade setuptools
USER model-server

We then copy training outputs into the model-server directory which is the directory for TorchServe. Training outputs were previously copied into the build directory from the Cloud Storage bucket (outputs of training run) by running the script “copy_artifacts.sh”. To instantiate and use the model in our TorchServe container we also need the helpers directory from our model training code base. To be able to use all files in this directory with TorchServe without explicitly listing them in the Dockerfile we create a zip archive. The reason for this is that when running the torch-model-archiver command later we cannot set an entire directory as the value in the --extra-files argument.

COPY ./custom_handler.py /home/model-server/
COPY ./model.pt /home/model-server/
COPY ./helpers.zip /home/model-server/
COPY ./label_map.json /home/model-server/
# copy_artifacts.sh

gsutil -m cp -r $_MODEL_DIR/* $_BUILD_DIR/.
mv `ls $_BUILD_DIR/*.pt | head -1` $_BUILD_DIR/model.pt

mv $_BUILD_DIR/$_LABEL_MAP_FILE $_BUILD_DIR/label_map.json

cp -r $_TRAINER_CODE_DIR/helpers $_BUILD_DIR/helpers

pushd $_BUILD_DIR; zip -r helpers.zip helpers; popd

echo `ls $_BUILD_DIR`

echo "copied artifacts to build dir"

Next we define the serving configuration such as health check and prediction listener ports for TorchServe and store it in a file named “config.properties”.

# create torchserve configuration file
USER root
RUN printf "
service_envelope=json" >> /home/model-server/config.properties
RUN printf "
inference_address=http://0.0.0.0:7080" >> /home/model-server/config.properties
RUN printf "
management_address=http://0.0.0.0:7081" >> /home/model-server/config.properties
USER model-server

# expose health and prediction listener ports from the image
EXPOSE 7080
EXPOSE 7081

We now run the torch-model-archiver command to package all model artifacts into a single model archive file. As mentioned above we list the “helpers.zip” archive as an extra file so it is available to us in the serving container. The model archive is saved in the “model-store” directory as “$_MODEL_NAME.mar”.

# create model archive file packaging model artifacts and dependencies
RUN torch-model-archiver -f \
    --model-name=$_MODEL_NAME \
    --version=1.0 \
    --serialized-file=/home/model-server/model.pt \
    --handler=/home/model-server/custom_handler.py \
    --extra-files "/home/model-server/helpers.zip,/home/model-server/label_map.json" \
    --export-path=/home/model-server/model-store

Finally we launch a TorchServe HTTP server to enable serving of the model referencing the configuration properties and the model archive file. As an alternative to “all” we could specify the model archive file directly like “$_MODEL_NAME=$_MODEL_NAME.mar”.

# run Torchserve HTTP serve to respond to prediction requests
CMD ["torchserve", \
    "--start", \
    "--ts-config=/home/model-server/config.properties", \
    "--models", \
    "all", \
    "--model-store", \
    "/home/model-server/model-store"]

Model Handler

An important component we need for TorchServe is a Python script that you package with the model when you use the model archiver. TorchServe executes this code when it runs. This script performs the following functions:

  • Initialize the model instance
  • Pre-process input data before it is sent to the model for inference
  • Customize how the model is invoked for inference
  • Post-process output from the model before sending back a response

TorchServe provides a BaseHandler class which provides methods for all of this functionality. We can inherit from this base class and override the methods with our own custom code. The handler receives two types of input:

  • data — the input data from the incoming request
  • context — the TorchServe context. You can use the following information for customization: model_name, model_dir, manifest, batch_size, gpu etc.

Below is the code for our custom handler class

import zipfile
with zipfile.ZipFile("helpers.zip","r") as zip_ref:
    zip_ref.extractall(".")

import json
import os
import logging
import torch
from ts.torch_handler.base_handler import BaseHandler
from transformers import BertTokenizer

from os import listdir
from os.path import isfile, join

from helpers.model import BertClf


class ModelHandler(BaseHandler):
    """
    A custom model handler implementation.
    """

    def __init__(self):
        super(ModelHandler, self).__init__()
        self.initialized = False
        self.manifest = None
        self.model = None
        self.device = None

    def initialize(self, context):
        """
        Loads the model.bin file and initializes the model object.
        Instantiates Tokenizer for preprocessor to use
        Modify the self.model = ... line to load the model in a
        correct manner.
        """
        
        # Parse context and set attributes
        self.manifest = context.manifest
        serialized_file = self.manifest["model"]["serializedFile"]
        properties = context.system_properties
        model_dir = properties.get("model_dir")

        # Set device to GPU if cuda available else CPU
        self.device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")

        # Find .bin or .pt file
        model_path = os.path.join(model_dir, serialized_file)
        if not os.path.isfile(model_path):
            raise RuntimeError("Missing the model.pt or pytorch_model.bin file")

        # Load model
        self.model = BertClf.load_checkpoint(model_path)
        self.model.to(self.device)
        self.model.eval()
        
        # Load tokenizer
        self.tokenizer = BertTokenizer.from_pretrained(self.model.model_name)
        
        # load mapping file
        with open("label_map.json", "r") as f:
            self.label_map = {int(k):v for k,v in json.load(f).items()}

        self.initialized = True


    def preprocess(self, data):
        """
        Transform raw input into model input data.
        Args:
            batch: list of raw requests, should match batch size
        Returns:
            list of preprocessed model input data
        """
        print(f"input data:
{data}")
        
        texts = []
        for i,d in enumerate(data):
            texts.append(d.get("text"))
        
        text_inputs = self.tokenizer(
            texts, padding=True, truncation=True, return_tensors="pt"
        )
        
        return text_inputs


    def inference(self, text_inputs):
        """
        Internal inference methods
        Args:
            model_input: preprocessed model input data
        Returns:
            list of inference output in NDArray
        """
        
        with torch.no_grad():
            return self.model(
                input_ids=text_inputs['input_ids'].to(self.device)
            ).cpu()

  
    def postprocess(self, model_output, data):
        """
        Return postprocessed inference result.
        Args:
            inference_output: list of inference output
        Returns:
            list of postprocessed results
        """
        prediction = [[self.label_map[i] for i, logit in enumerate(logits) if logit>0] for logits in model_output]
        
        processed_prediction = []
        for i,p in enumerate(prediction):
            d = {
                "pred": p,
                "pred_raw": model_output[i].tolist(),
                "id": data[i].get("id")
            }
            processed_prediction.append(d)
        
        return processed_prediction


    def handle(self, data, context):
        """
        Invoked by TorchServe for prediction request.
        Do pre-processing of data, prediction using model and postprocessing of prediciton output
        Note that this function can be omitted.
        Args:
            data: Input data for prediction
            context: Initial context contains model server system properties.
        Returns:
            prediction output
        """
        text_inputs = self.preprocess(data)
        model_output = self.inference(text_inputs)
        return self.postprocess(model_output, data)

Since we had to create a zip archive for the helpers directory to pass it to the model archiver we need to now unzip it to be able to import from it. I won’t go into more detail for the code of the handler class here as I think most of it is self explanatory.

Setting up the Dockerfile and custom handler are the most complicated parts for this step. In our “main.py” file (shown above) we simply run a build trigger which we defined in Google Cloud Build using the Cloud Build Python SDK. The resulting TorchServe container image uri and the commit_sha are passed to the next step.

deploy_model

def deploy_model(
    comp_params: dict,
    endpoint_image_uri: str,
    commit_sha: str
) -> NamedTuple('deploy_model_outputs', [
    ('model_resource_name', str)
]):
    
    import argparse
    from google.cloud import aiplatform
    
    cfg = argparse.Namespace(**comp_params)
    
    aiplatform.init(project=cfg.project_id, location=cfg.model_location)
    
    model_kwargs = {
        "serving_container_image_uri": endpoint_image_uri + ":" + commit_sha,
        "serving_container_predict_route": f"{cfg.endpoint_predict_route}/{cfg.endpoint_model_name}",
        "serving_container_health_route": cfg.endpoint_health_route,
        "serving_container_ports": [7080]
    }

    try:
        parent_model = [x for x in aiplatform.Model.list() if x.display_name == cfg.endpoint_model_name][0]
        model_kwargs["parent_model"] = parent_model.resource_name
    except IndexError:
        model_kwargs["display_name"] = cfg.endpoint_model_name

    model = aiplatform.Model.upload(**model_kwargs)

    endpoint = aiplatform.Endpoint.create(
        display_name = cfg.endpoint_model_name,
        project = cfg.project_id,
        location = cfg.model_location
    )

    model.deploy(
        endpoint = endpoint,
        deployed_model_display_name = cfg.endpoint_model_name,
        machine_type = cfg.endpoint_machine_type
    )

    return (model.resource_name,)

Almost all of the heavy lifting for this pipeline was done by the train_model and build_model components. For deploying the model we run some commands from the Vertex AI Python SDK to upload the model to the model registry, create an endpoint and deploy the model to it. There is also pre-built components that could be used for these steps.

save_model_info

def save_model_info(
    comp_params: dict,
    model_info: dict,
    model_resource_name: str
) -> NamedTuple('save_model_info_outputs', [
    ('DUMMY', str)
]):

    import argparse
    import json
    from google.cloud import storage as gcs
    
    cfg = argparse.Namespace(**comp_params)

    model_info["model_resource_name"] = model_resource_name

    client = gcs.Client(project=cfg.project_id)
    bucket_name = cfg.bucket.split("gs://")[-1]
    bucket = client.bucket(bucket_name)
    
    # contains information for latest model
    target_dir = f"{cfg.model_info_dir}/{cfg.language}/{cfg.language}_{{}}"
    # working dir of current training run    
    wd = f"{cfg.working_dir[len(cfg.bucket)+1:]}/{{}}"

    # copy mapping objects created during training to model info dir
    # https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/copying-renaming-moving-objects#storage-copy-object-python
    blob_model_info = bucket.blob(wd.format(cfg.output_file_model_info))
    blob_model_info.upload_from_string(json.dumps(model_info))
    bucket.copy_blob(blob_model_info, bucket, target_dir.format(cfg.output_file_model_info))
    
    return ("DONE",)

In a last step we store some information about parameters used to train the model as well as the model registry resource name to a file in Google Cloud Storage. This way we can always just have a look into this file to know which is the latest model we should use for inference.

Inference

Once we deployed our model to an endpoint we can use it for inference. Either through the UI:

or alternatively you can use the Python SDK:

from google.cloud import aiplatform

def endpoint_predict_sample(
    project: str, location: str, instances: list, endpoint: str
):
    aiplatform.init(project=project, location=location)

    endpoint = aiplatform.Endpoint(endpoint)

    prediction = endpoint.predict(instances=instances)
    print(prediction)
    return prediction

project = ""
location = ""
endpoint = ""

instances = [{"text": "I hate you."}, {"text": "I love you."}]

endpoint_predict_sample(project, location, instances, endpoint)

Conclusion

The goal of this article is to help others to get a PyTorch training pipeline to run on Google Vertex AI. There are a few building blocks that I had trouble figuring out at first and I hope by using my code as a template to build off of others wont have the same problems.

I should note that my implementation is focused on showcasing custom training with Pytorch and leaves out important ML Ops topics such as model testing and validation or hyperparameter tuning (which can all be integrated in Vertex AI workflows). Furthermore I am aware that for the topics, which I did include, my implementation definitely is not perfect and has room to improve. Therefore I am always happy about suggestions for improvements in the comments!

This article is the first in a two part series. In the next article I will show you how to integrate the model we trained in an automated prediction pipeline. See you there!

For everyone who just scrolled to the bottom right away, here is the git repository again on which this article is based on: https://github.com/sirluk/vertex_ai_pytorch

item.title: Adverserial Training
item.dc:creator: Lukas Hauzenberger
item.content:encoded:
Large language models following the transformer architecture have been incredibly successful since their introduction by Vaswani et. al. in 2018. They have given rise to large pre-trained models such as BERT (Devlin et. al., 2019) which can be finetuned and applied to a wide variety of language tasks. BERT provides rich text encoding vectors due to being trained on millions of rows of unlabeled text. There is many great articles on Transformers and BERT on the web so I wont go into further detail here.

Bias in Machine Learning

The way BERT is trained however is a gift and a curse. On the one hand training is unsupervised, therefore theoretically it can be fed an infinite number of text elements without any manual data labelling. In practice BERT was still trained on extremely large copora (English Wikipedia with 2,500M words and BooksCorpus with 800M words) which lead to the model becoming incredibly good at language understanding. On the other hand however “unsupervised” also means different types of bias that exist in a language such as race or gender bias can find their way into the model without any data quality checks. Various researchers such as Buolamwini & Gebru (Gender Shades study) have already shown that bias does in fact exist in modern Machine Learning systems and a number of methods have been introduced to combat bias at all stages of the Machine Learning workflow. Today I would like to shine the spotlight on one of them: Adverserial Training

Adverserial Training

Adverserial Training emerged from the field of domain adaptation where the technique was first described by Ganin & Lempitsky (2015). The basic idea is to reduce the impact of a pre-defined attribute (such as gender) on task predictions. To do that intermediate model outputs (such as BERT encodings) are fed into a task head as well as a second head which has the objective to predict this attribute. During the backward pass the sign of the gradients flowing back out of this head is reversed (in the gradient reversal layer or GRL for short). This has the effect of “punishing” the rest of the model for enabling correct domain predictions.

Adverserial training provides an elegant way to finetune a pre-trained language encoder model such as BERT while controlling for bias with respect to a specific attribute.

Pytorch Implementation

In the following section I will show you step by step how to implement the building blocks required for adversarial training in pytorch

  • Dataset
  • Gradient Reversal Layer
  • Adverserial head
  • Adjusted update step
  • Evaluation by adversarial attack

All the code examples are taken from this repository which I created to showcase adversarial training.

Dataset

I used the BIOS dataset (De-Arteaga et. al. 2019). It includes short biographies with two labels job title and gender. One datapoint contains the following information:

  • BIO: “dr practices at sai ram super speciality dental clinic in malkajgiri hyderabad completed bds from dr ntr university of health sciences andhra pradesh in”
  • TITLE: “dentist”
  • GENDER: “F”

Here title is the main classification objective and gender acts as the protected attribute. More information on how to get the data can be found in the README of the git repository.

Gradient Reversal Layer

Before we can build the adversarial head we need a simple class for the Gradient Reversal Layer which inherits from the autograd function class. Autograd functions enable you to define new operations for the forward and backward pass. In our case we only want to reverse the sign of the gradients flowing back out of the adversarial head in the backward pass which we achieve in the backward method as follows

Lambda here is an optional hyperparameter which we could use to also adjust the magnitude of the gradients. In my experiments however at best this did not have any effect, more commonly however it even reduced the effectiveness of adversarial training.

NOTE: A special quirk of autograd functions is that if you define no operation in the forward method the function does not modify the gradients in the backward method. For this reason we apply .view_as() which effectively leaves the input unchanged but still gets registered as an operation.

Adversarial Head

We can now use the GRL class to build the adverserial head. To keep focus on the important code snippets our adverserial head class inherits from a generic classifier head. I assume you are familiar with such heads but in the file model_heads.py in the repository you can find one simple and one more advanced version. Furthermore a common practice for the adverserial head is to have several classifiers side by side with loss averaging to increase robustness. You can see this in the _init_ method of the AdvHead class where I create a list of classifiers.

In the forward pass we iterate over the list of classifiers and pass the input (i.e. the BERT embeddings) to each of them. Before we do this however we apply the GRL class to the input. I put this in a separate method (forward_reverse) which wraps around the forward method because in some cases we might not need this functionality (for example at inference time). Here you can see the full AdvHead class:

Adjusted update step

In the file adv_model.py you can see how adversarial training is integrated into a classification model. One thing we need to do is to combine the loss from the task head with the loss from the adversarial head.

Furthermore I mentioned earlier that typically the adversarial head consists of several classifiers. Therefore we need a function to average the outputs before running the backward pass. This is what self._get_mean_loss() does

For evaluation however we do not average the loss but pick the mode of the predictions (majority vote).

NOTE: In general when using accuracy as the evaluation metric we strive to reach 50% accuracy on the protected attribute meaning random predictions i.e. no information about the attribute is contained in the model.

Evaluation by adversarial attack

We now already went over the essential components to make adversarial training work. The only thing left is to talk about evaluating how effective it is in actually removing information about the protected attribute from the encodings which are being fed into the classification head. A common thing to do is to run an adversarial attack. For this you first freeze the encoder model and with it the encodings. With a newly initialized adverserial head you then try to predict the protected attribute (This is now also a use case where we do not need the forward_reverse method from the adversarial head and can use the forward method). The idea is to show how much information about the protected attribute is still contained in the embeddings after adversarial training.

For the BIOS dataset I ran two experiments which can be found here

  • experiment with adverserial training:
    adverserial-bert_uncased_L-2_H-128_A-2–64–2e-05-seed0
  • experiment without adverserial training:
    task-bert_uncased_L-2_H-128_A-2–64–2e-05-seed0

When looking at the results you can see that the metric “acc_adv_attack” is considerably lower for the model trained with adversarial training (orange line). At the same time task accuracy stays at a similar level.

Final thoughts / things to consider

While adversarial training can work quite well there is some things to consider before applying it

  • One thing to consider is the time investment needed for data labelling. Adversarial training requires additional labels for each protected attribute we want to remove / control.
  • A second thing to take care of is to ensure that the training dataset is relatively balanced in terms of task and protected labels. This means that there should exist equal amount of each protected class within each task class. Otherwise the model could learn that one protected class is more likely overall than the others and by only predicting this one could reach an accuracy above 50%.

I hope you enjoyed this article and that it maybe helps you implement adversarial training yourself!

I already mentioned the repository with all the code in the article but since I know some of you might scroll to the bottom right away here it is again: link

References

[1] Vaswani, A., Shazeer, N., Parmar, N., Uszkoreit, J., Jones, L., Gomez, A. N., Kaiser, L. & Polosukhin, I. (2017). Attention is All you Need. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems. Volume 30.

[2] Devlin, J., Chang, M., Lee, K. & Toutanova, K. (2019). BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding. Proceedings of the 2019 Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies, Volume 1.

[3] Buolamwini, J. & Gebru, T. (2018). Gender Shades: Intersectional Accuracy Disparities in Commercial Gender Classification. Proceedings of the 1st Conference on Fairness, Accountability and Transparency. Volume 81.

[4] Ganin, Y. & Lempitsky, V. (2015). Unsupervised domain adaptation by backpropagation. International conference on machine learning.

item.title: An practical introduction to Diff-Pruning for BERT
item.dc:creator: Lukas Hauzenberger
item.content:encoded:
In this article I would like to give a short introduction for an elegant technique to make finetuning of large language models more storage efficient. From my own experience it is often the case that one has several instances of BERT stored on disk which only differ in terms of how much the weights were changed during task-adaptation. Diff-Pruning, which was developed by Guo et. al. in 2021 is a training technique which aims at tackling this problem. The basic idea of Diff-Pruning is to limit the amount of weights which are adapted during finetuning of a pre-trained model and to only store the difference of weights compared to their pre-trained state. The loss in performance compared to full finetuning was shown to be very minimal even with only .5% of the parameters of a full BERT_large model.

I came across Diff Pruning when I was looking at different sparsification techniques for a research project I am involved in. Unfortunately the code from the authors was set up in a way that it was difficult for me to integrate and expand which is why I decided to create my own Pytorch implementation from scratch. After a quick conceptual overview of the ideas presented in the paper, I will use my re-implementation in this article to explain how Diff-Pruning works in practice. The code from the original paper can be found on github.

What is Diff-Pruning

As already mentioned Diff-Pruning tries reduce the number of weights that get changed during finetuning of a pre-trained language model like BERT. It is important to note that it does not try to reduce or change the pre-trained model weights in any way. For this reason, a first important step for Diff-Pruning is to not think of just the set of model weights θ_pre that get changed during finetuning to task-specific θ_τ but to think of separate fixed pre-trained weight values θ_pre and task-specific “diff”-values δ_τ.

instead of

The initial state of all weights in δ_τ is 0. We now want to limit the number of δ_τ,i which change to non-zero value during training. This constraint can be expressed as a L0 penalty in the loss function.

For the set of parameters δ_τ the term 1{δ_τ,i≠0} equals 1 if δ_τ,i is non-zero. L is some Loss function, d represents the total number of parameters in the model and λ is a hyperparameter to control the degree of regularization. Since this penalty term is not differentiable however, it poses a challenge for training using gradient techniques. Thankfully there is a solution to this problem which was initially proposed by Louizos et. al. in 2018. They approximate the L0 objective via stochastic gates to make it differentiable. Stochastic gates in neural networks make use of the reparameterization trick (Kingma and Welling, 2014). Explaining the details about how it works would go beyond the scope of this article but there is a great many resources only which do just that, for example this one.

L0 Regularization

In principle, approximate L0 regularization works as follows:

1. Construct a mask z via a parametrized distribution called hard-concrete distribution

u is drawn from a uniform distribution and log(α) is the distribution parameter which is optimized together with the model weights during training. Typically for each parameter value in the model, a separate value for log(α) is learned. l and r are fixed hyperparameters which are typically set to -1.5 and 1.5 for Diff-Pruning. (Remark: the distribution features a second learnable parameter β which was disregarded, i.e. set to 1 for Diff-Pruning, I assume to simplify the calculations)

2. The z-mask which will be either 0 or 1 for the most part due to the hard sigmoid gate. It is incorporated in the model parameters as follows:
